main.title: Ni no Kuni: Wrath of the White Witch
main.subtitle: A boy looks for another world
main.summary: Ni no Kuni: Wrath of the White Witch is Level-5's role-playing adventure, first released for PlayStation 3 in Japan on 17 November 2011. Oliver travels to another world hoping to save his mother, accompanied by the fairy Drippy. A story rooted in grief opens into colourful towns, strange creatures and a wider struggle against dark powers. Studio Ghibli produced the animated sequences, while Joe Hisaishi contributed to the score. The world connects the appearance of an animated film with an adventure that gives the player time to explore its places.

cards.heading: A boy looks for another world
cards.text: Ni no Kuni: Wrath of the White Witch is Level-5's role-playing adventure, first released for PlayStation 3 in Japan on 17 November 2011. Oliver travels to another world hoping to save his mother, accompanied by the fairy Drippy. A story rooted in grief opens into colourful towns, strange creatures and a wider struggle against dark powers. Studio Ghibli produced the animated sequences, while Joe Hisaishi contributed to the score. The world connects the appearance of an animated film with an adventure that gives the player time to explore its places.

cards.heading: Fight beside a familiar
cards.text: Battles let Oliver and his companions move around an encounter while choosing attacks, spells and defensive actions. Familiars offer another way to participate: the player can train and develop creatures with different strengths, then bring them into the fighting. Their abilities make building a group a continuing part of the journey rather than a decision made only when a new human companion arrives. Recovering resources and choosing when to switch actions remain important, so the friendly presentation accompanies a system that asks the player to learn how the party works.

cards.heading: Travel gives the story its scale
cards.text: Oliver's journey begins on foot and later gains other forms of travel, including a boat and a dragon. Those changes turn distant parts of the world map into places the party can finally reach. Towns provide smaller requests and encounters between the larger events, keeping Oliver's wish connected to people he meets along the way. Written by Akihiro Hino, the PlayStation 3 game expanded the earlier Japanese Nintendo DS adventure. Western releases arrived in 2013, and later versions brought its story and world to further platforms.

main.title: Minecraft
main.subtitle: A world becomes a set of materials
main.summary: Mining, making and sharing turn a landscape into an ongoing collective project.

cards.heading: The public beginnings of Minecraft
cards.text: Markus Persson made an early Minecraft version public on May 17, 2009, when the project was still close to its beginnings as Cave Game. Terrain built from removable and replaceable blocks supplied the foundation for construction and survival. Public development continued until version 1.0 in 2011, with player communities finding their own purposes for the same materials.

cards.heading: One block, one common rule
cards.text: Dirt, stone and wood share the same block scale. Breaking and placing them can make shelters, stairs, bridges and much larger buildings. The straightforward units make it possible to plan a structure a little at a time, while the number of available combinations leaves room for elaborate projects.

cards.heading: Night creates the first objective
cards.text: The day-night cycle gives Survival players an early reason to gather materials. Darkness brings hostile creatures, making a shelter useful before the first night ends. Building becomes a way to protect the player as well as change the landscape. Later tools and systems provide more ways to manage those threats.

cards.heading: Recipes connect the materials
cards.text: Crafting recipes convert materials into tools and other objects. Wood becomes planks, planks become sticks and those components become tools that reach further resources. Learning the relationships between materials opens new possibilities for building and survival, with recipes often shared between players.

cards.heading: From a prototype to a shared culture
cards.text: Minecraft was available in public development before the release of version 1.0 in 2011. Its blocks give terrain a consistent grammar: an object can be removed, carried and placed somewhere else. The game grew from Markus Persson's early work into a wider Mojang production and a vast player culture. Buildings, servers, technical contraptions, lessons and videos extend its history far beyond one official set of objectives.

features.title: A world made together
features.summary: Players helped shape Minecraft's creative building, custom textures and multiplayer tools.

cards.heading: Players inspire Creative mode and custom textures
cards.text: In his February 2011 postmortem, Markus Persson describes players finding purposes in Minecraft that he had not originally prioritized. Free building from an early engine test became Creative mode because people continued to enjoy it. He also recalls changing his mind about custom textures after seeing a player made Portal server. The work arriving from outside the studio could make an argument through something playable. A modification showed what an option might accomplish more directly than a request for another feature alone could do.

cards.heading: Moving inventories onto multiplayer servers
cards.text: Persson's account also identifies the cost of postponing multiplayer during a rewrite. New systems had accumulated assumptions about a single player, mixing parts of their rules with the code that drew them. Moving inventory to the server required substantial further work. Shared building therefore depended on less visible agreements beneath the blocks. The software had to determine which state belonged to everyone, rather than letting each screen behave like a complete private world. His postmortem describes a change toward testing new features in both modes earlier.

cards.heading: Building one block at a time
cards.text: Jens Bergensten explains another shared rule in a 2016 interview: building remains an action involving one block at a time. An efficient editor could place more at once, but he wanted another person to understand a construction as it happened. Two builders could also work faster together. The limit gives collaboration an immediately visible form. Someone can follow the next placement, contribute a neighbouring piece and recognize how an unfinished structure is becoming a larger plan through actions that remain small enough to read.

cards.heading: Saving materials in the toolbar
cards.text: A 2017 snapshot announcement shows another scale of improvement. Creative players could save and reload toolbars, preserving a chosen set of materials instead of repeatedly assembling it. The same experimental release introduced concrete, concrete powder and glazed terracotta. The publication asks players to report bugs and protect their worlds before testing. New building possibilities arrived alongside a practical testing routine. A public update could supply tools for making things while also inviting the audience to help discover how those tools behaved outside the development team's own examples.

main.title: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword
main.summary: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword is a 2011 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Wii.

cards.heading: Link between Skyloft and the world below
cards.text: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword is a 2011 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Wii. A mainline entry in The Legend of Zelda series, Skyward Sword is the first game in the Zelda timeline, and details the origins of the Triforce and the Master Sword. The series' main protagonist Link, a resident of a floating town called Skyloft, sets out to rescue his childhood friend Zelda after she is kidnapped and brought to the abandoned lands below the clouds. As Link, players navigate Skyloft and the lands below it, completing quests that advance the story and solving environmental and dungeon-based puzzles. The mechanics and combat, the latter focusing on attacking and blocking with sword and shield, are reliant on the Wii MotionPlus peripheral.

cards.heading: Five years of development and the MotionPlus challenge
cards.text: Development took around five years, beginning after the release of Twilight Princess in 2006. Multiple earlier Zelda games influenced the developers, including Twilight Princess, Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask. Many aspects of the game's overworld and gameplay were designed to streamline and populate the experience for players. The art style was influenced by the work of impressionist and post-impressionist painters, including Paul Cézanne. The implementation of Wii MotionPlus proved problematic for the developers, to the point where it was nearly discarded. It was the first Zelda game to use a live orchestra for the majority of its tracks, with music composed by a team led by Hajime Wakai and supervised by Koji Kondo.

cards.heading: Success, criticism and influence on later games
cards.text: Announced in 2009, Skyward Sword was planned for release in 2010 but was delayed to November 2011 to further refine and expand it. It was a critical and commercial success, receiving perfect scores from multiple journalistic sites, winning and receiving nominations for numerous industry and journalist awards, and selling over three million copies worldwide. However, critics and series fans expressed criticism over its excessive linearity and backtracking, its motion controls, a general lack of innovation in the gameplay and were divided on its narrative choices. Feedback on the game later influenced the development of future Zelda games, including A Link Between Worlds and the next entry for home consoles Breath of the Wild.

cards.heading: The high-definition return on Switch
cards.text: A high-definition remaster of the game, The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword HD, was co-developed by Tantalus Media and released for the Nintendo Switch in July 2021. As of March 2022, the remaster had sold nearly 4 million units worldwide.

main.title: Mario Kart 7
main.summary: Mario Kart 7 is a 2011 kart racing game developed by Nintendo EAD in cooperation with Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS.

cards.heading: Seventeen drivers and thirty-two courses
cards.text: Mario Kart 7 is a 2011 kart racing game developed by Nintendo EAD in cooperation with Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS. In Mario Kart 7, the player takes control of one of seventeen Mario series characters, who participate in races on various Mario-themed race tracks using specialized items to hinder opponents or gain advantages. In single player mode, players can race against computer-controlled characters in 8 multi-race cups consisting of 32 tracks (4 in each cup) over three difficulty levels. Alternatively, players can race against the clock in a Time Trial mode.

cards.heading: Gliders, gyroscopes and eight-player races
cards.text: New additions to Mario Kart 7 include hang-gliding attachments for karts (which introduced aerial sections to race tracks for the first time in the series), the ability to drive in first person, gyro controls, and the ability to customize the vehicles' builds. Additionally, Mario Kart 7 supports both local and online multiplayer through Nintendo Network for up to eight players. The ability to play online was discontinued on April 8, 2024, along with Nintendo Network as a whole.

cards.heading: Developing with Retro Studios and success on 3DS
cards.text: Development of Mario Kart 7 began in early 2010 as a port of Mario Kart Wii. Producer Hideki Konno said that completing the game was an "act of emergency" due to low 3DS sales at that time and because of the very few staff involved in its development. In the end, Retro Studios was involved in the development of the retro tracks (tracks from prior games in the series). Mario Kart 7 received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised its innovations, race tracks, and gyro control option. The game has won several awards and was a commercial success, becoming the best-selling game on the Nintendo 3DS with nearly 19 million copies sold.

main.title: Final Fantasy XIII-2
main.summary: Final Fantasy XIII-2 is a 2011 role-playing video game developed and published by Square Enix for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360.

cards.heading: Serah and Noel travel through time
cards.text: Final Fantasy XIII-2 is a 2011 role-playing video game developed and published by Square Enix for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. It was released in 2011 in Japan and 2012 in North America and PAL regions, and was ported to Windows in 2014. XIII-2 is a direct sequel to the 2009 role-playing game Final Fantasy XIII and part of the Fabula Nova Crystallis subseries. It includes modified features from the previous game, including fast-paced combat and a customizable "Paradigm" system to control which abilities are used by the characters, and adds a new system that allows monsters to be captured and used in battle. The game's plot features a heavy time travel element, allowing the player to jump between different times at the same location or different places at the same time. Lightning, the protagonist of the original game, has disappeared into an unknown world. Her younger sister Serah Farron and Noel Kreiss journey through time in an attempt to find her.

cards.heading: A year and a half to rethink the sequel
cards.text: Development of Final Fantasy XIII-2 began in early 2010 and lasted about one and a half years. The game was unveiled at the Square Enix 1st Production Department Premier in January 2011. Many of the key designers remained in their roles from the previous game, and developer tri-Ace was hired to help with the game's design, art, and programming. The development team wanted to exceed Final Fantasy XIII in every aspect while making the story's tone more dark and mysterious than the previous game. The game builds upon the Paradigm Shift battle system used in XIII and includes a less linear overall design.

cards.heading: Reception and the road to Lightning Returns
cards.text: Final Fantasy XIII-2 received critical acclaim in Japan and generally positive reviews from Western video game journalists. Though praised for its gameplay, lack of linearity, and graphics, the game's story was criticized as weak and confusing. The game was the fifth-best selling game of 2011 in Japan, and sold 3.1 million copies worldwide by January 2013. A sequel, Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII, was released in 2013 in Japan and 2014 worldwide.

cards.heading: Backward compatibility, 4K and FPS Boost
cards.text: The game was added to Xbox One backward compatibility along with its predecessor and sequel in November 2018. It is also Xbox One X Enhanced, allowing it to display in 4K Ultra HD. In November 2021, support for FPS Boost on Xbox Series X/S was added allowing it to run at 60 frames per second.

main.title: Uncharted: Golden Abyss
main.summary: Uncharted: Golden Abyss is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Bend Studio and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation Vita.

cards.heading: Drake and Chase search for Quivira
cards.text: Uncharted: Golden Abyss is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Bend Studio and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation Vita. A spin-off of Naughty Dog's Uncharted series, the game was released as a launch title for the console. Golden Abyss is a prequel to the series, taking place before the events of Uncharted: Drake's Fortune. The story revolves around adventurer-treasure hunter Nathan Drake as he becomes involved in a search for the lost city of Quivira and is aided by fellow treasure hunter Marisa Chase. Gameplay combines action-adventure with platforming elements, with players solving puzzles and fighting enemies using cover-based third-person shooting.

cards.heading: Bend Studio works with Naughty Dog
cards.text: Concept work for Golden Abyss began in 2007, when Sony asked Bend Studio to develop a new Uncharted as a console launch title. Due to the changing specifications of the Vita, much of the early development was done using PlayStation 3 hardware. The entire project was overseen by original developer Naughty Dog, with Bend Studio receiving assets from the first two Uncharted titles and getting access to their motion capture facilities. John Garvin was both director and scriptwriter, the latter under the supervision of main series writer Amy Hennig. Hennig also ensured the return of Nolan North as Drake and Richard McGonagle as Sully.

cards.heading: Reception and Vita exclusivity
cards.text: The game was revealed in January 2011 alongside the Vita. Golden Abyss debuted to strong sales and generally positive critical reception. Journalists praised its graphics, voice performances, and recreation of Uncharted gameplay on the platform. Criticism focused on its storyline and implementation of Vita-specific controls. To date, the game remains exclusive to the platform, as it was left out of the PlayStation 4's Uncharted: The Nathan Drake Collection due to the standalone nature of its narrative.

main.title: Ridge Racer
main.summary: Ridge Racer, originally named Ridge Racer Vita, is a 2011 racing video game published by Namco Bandai Games for the PlayStation Vita as a launch title, originally on 17 December 2011 in Japan, and internationally from February 2012.

cards.heading: Ridge Racer joins the Vita launch
cards.text: Ridge Racer, originally named Ridge Racer Vita, is a 2011 racing video game published by Namco Bandai Games for the PlayStation Vita as a launch title, originally on 17 December 2011 in Japan, and internationally from February 2012. It is the 5th handheld game in the Ridge Racer series and the first on a Sony platform since 2006's Ridge Racer 2. It was the first and only game in the series developed by Cellius. The game continues the Ridge Racer tradition of arcade racing and supports single-player as well as local and Wi-Fi multiplayer games. Upon release, Ridge Racer was mostly panned by video game critics due to the lack of a career mode and particularly the lack of content, with much of it locked as paid downloadable content.

cards.heading: Drifting, nitro and eight-player races
cards.text: Drifting around corners preserves speed and charges nitro. Following closely behind another car adds a slipstream boost. Spot Race, Time Attack and World Race provide the main events, with local wireless and online competition alongside solo play. Race credits buy car upgrades.

cards.heading: Downloadable cars, courses and music
cards.text: The Hornet from Sega's Daytona USA makes a cameo appearance as available DLC, as well as an exclusive song (with lyrics by Takenobu Mitsuyoshi) and course inspired by both franchises. Other cameos include cars with paint schemes derived from The Idolmaster, as well as DoCoMO and Pac-Man-themed versions of the Kamata SYNCi, the game's cover car. The DoCoMo and Idolmaster cars are not available outside Japan. Other downloadable content include new cars and courses, as well as music tracks from previous entries in the franchise.

main.title: Super Stardust Delta
main.subtitle: A planet becomes a shooting arena
main.summary: Super Stardust Delta is Housemarque's PlayStation Vita arcade shooter, first released in Japan on 19 January 2012. The player guides a small ship around a planet while asteroids and enemies occupy the surrounding orbit. The Vita's two analogue sticks separate movement from firing, allowing the ship to escape in one direction while clearing another. A curved playfield keeps the action contained without making it flat. The player is continually looking for a safer route through a space that is being filled and broken apart by incoming objects and weapon fire.

cards.heading: A planet becomes a shooting arena
cards.text: Super Stardust Delta is Housemarque's PlayStation Vita arcade shooter, first released in Japan on 19 January 2012. The player guides a small ship around a planet while asteroids and enemies occupy the surrounding orbit. The Vita's two analogue sticks separate movement from firing, allowing the ship to escape in one direction while clearing another. A curved playfield keeps the action contained without making it flat. The player is continually looking for a safer route through a space that is being filled and broken apart by incoming objects and weapon fire.

cards.heading: Change the weapon when the target changes
cards.text: Ice and Fire weapons have different strengths against the objects appearing in the field, making quick switching part of an efficient defence. Pickups strengthen the ship, while bombs offer a way to recover when the surrounding space becomes difficult to read. Different bomb effects connect to the Vita's touch and motion inputs, adding another response beyond the two sticks. The player has to recognise when ordinary movement and firing can still solve the situation and when a stronger intervention is needed to reopen a useful path through the debris.

cards.heading: An arcade series uses the Vita's controls
cards.text: Harri Tikkanen directed the game and Ari Pulkkinen composed its music. The main arcade mode contains five planets divided into phases, each concluding with a boss. North American and PAL releases followed in February 2012 around the handheld's wider launch. Housemarque adapted a familiar series to a machine whose paired sticks could preserve its immediate control while touch surfaces supplied additional effects. The result offers a compact demonstration of the Vita's possibilities without losing the central arcade task: stay alive, remove the next threat and keep enough of the orbit clear to continue moving.

main.title: Wipeout 2048
main.subtitle: Anti-gravity racing before the familiar future
main.summary: Wipeout 2048 is Studio Liverpool's PlayStation Vita racing game, first released in Japan on 19 January 2012. Set before the original Wipeout, its championship runs through the years 2048 to 2050, bringing anti-gravity craft into streets that still resemble a recognisable city. The tracks therefore sit between ordinary urban roads and the more distant future associated with the series. Racing keeps the familiar combination of high speed, airbrakes and weapons, with the Vita's screen presenting the movement in the player's hands rather than across a television.

cards.heading: Anti-gravity racing before the familiar future
cards.text: Wipeout 2048 is Studio Liverpool's PlayStation Vita racing game, first released in Japan on 19 January 2012. Set before the original Wipeout, its championship runs through the years 2048 to 2050, bringing anti-gravity craft into streets that still resemble a recognisable city. The tracks therefore sit between ordinary urban roads and the more distant future associated with the series. Racing keeps the familiar combination of high speed, airbrakes and weapons, with the Vita's screen presenting the movement in the player's hands rather than across a television.

cards.heading: Turn with the whole width of the track
cards.text: The craft float above the course, so steering involves anticipating their movement instead of simply pointing at a corner. Airbrakes help tighten a line, while speed pads reward positioning before the next turn. Weapon pickups can change the balance between protecting a lead and interrupting an opponent. The player gradually learns where the track offers room for a correction and where a poor approach becomes a collision. Different event conditions make those same routes serve more than a conventional race against a full field of competitors.

cards.heading: A new handheld, a final Studio Liverpool game
cards.text: Wipeout 2048 was developed alongside the Vita's arrival and became one of the handheld's launch titles. Its online features included interaction with Wipeout HD on PlayStation 3, linking the portable release to an existing community. Reviewers praised the presentation while noting long loading times and other technical compromises. The game was Studio Liverpool's final production before the studio closed in 2012. Its tracks later joined Wipeout HD and the Fury expansion in the PlayStation 4 Omega Collection, giving this earlier chapter of the fictional championship another home.

main.title: Resident Evil: Revelations
main.subtitle: Jill and Chris investigate a virus at sea
main.summary: Resident Evil: Revelations is a 2012 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the Nintendo 3DS.

cards.heading: Jill and Chris investigate a virus at sea
cards.text: Resident Evil: Revelations is a 2012 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the Nintendo 3DS. Set shortly after Resident Evil 4, it follows counter-terrorism agents Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield as they try to uncover the truth behind a bioterrorist organization that plans to infect the Earth's oceans with a virus. In the single-player mode, the player must complete a series of episodes that involve solving puzzles and defeating enemies. In the multiplayer, players may fight their way through altered single-player scenarios.

cards.heading: Limited resources bring survival back
cards.text: Revelations emphasizes survival, evasion, and exploration over fast-paced combat by providing the player with limited ammunition, health, and movement speed. It was designed to bring back the content and horror of the Resident Evil roots, while at the same time trying to modernize the gameplay. Revelations was also the first game to support the Nintendo 3DS Circle Pad Pro outside Japan. The game was a moderate commercial success and received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised its spooky setting, sound direction, and presentation. Criticism was targeted at its inconsistent gameplay between episodes. The game received three nominations at the Golden Joystick Awards, including Ultimate Game of the Year, and was nominated for Handheld Game of the Year at the 16th Annual D.I.C.E. Awards.

cards.heading: Genesis uncovers hidden supplies
cards.text:
Resident Evil: Revelations is a survival horror game where the player must complete a series of scenarios collected together into episodes. Although most scenarios involve the player controlling Jill Valentine aboard a ghost ship, some require the player to control other characters in different settings. To progress through a scenario, the player must complete a number of objectives, ranging from solving puzzles to defeating bosses, collecting keys that open doors to new areas, and reaching a specific point.

As Jill, the player can upgrade firearms by finding special items. The player may also perform melee attacks when an enemy has been stunned after being shot at the right time. Ammunition and health items are dispersed to help players manage their resources. A device called Genesis can be used to scan and find hidden items in nearby environments. An automap feature is available to help players navigate.

cards.heading: The 3DS game reaches home systems
cards.text: A high-definition (HD) version was released for Windows, PlayStation 3, Wii U, and Xbox 360 in 2013, and for PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Nintendo Switch in 2017. This version does not support the 3D capabilities of the Nintendo 3DS but features enhanced graphics and additional content, including a new difficulty setting. Across all platforms, the HD version sold more than two million copies worldwide, but was criticized for its dated graphics and uneven controls. Resident Evil: Revelations 2 was released in 2015.
